S&P 500 Classification

Fred Viole

24 April, 2026

Intro

We are going to define a function for comparing a time-series for its most representative counterpart in a reference time-series(s). This expands the analysis already presented in “Time-Series Classification” by using vectors of different lengths for partial time-series matching.

In this example we will ascertain the most similar period for the S&P 500 index since 1950 to the current year 2026 returns through April, 2026.

Load Required Packages in R

#require(devtools); install_github('OVVO-Financial/NNS', ref = "NNS-Beta-Version")
require(NNS)
require(data.table)
require(quantmod)
require(zoo)

Get data

We will load the data for the S&P 500 index from 1950. This will create the variable GSPC. Further, we will create:

  1. A daily return based dataset: current_returns & reference_returns
  2. A dataset of closing prices: current & reference
  3. A window length: w
# Download data
getSymbols('^GSPC', src='yahoo', from=as.Date("1950-01-01"))
## [1] "GSPC"
# Drop first observation: dailyReturn() sets it to 0 (no prior price)
GSPC <- GSPC[-1]

# Create reference distribution (arithmetic returns, explicit)
reference_returns <- dailyReturn(GSPC, type = "arithmetic")
reference <- GSPC$GSPC.Adjusted

# Create current distribution (or sub in another period)
current_year <- year(Sys.Date())
current_returns <- reference_returns[as.character(current_year)]
current <- reference[as.character(current_year)]

# Window length
w <- length(current_returns)

Which Calendar Year is Most Similar?

Let’s identify the calendar year which is most similar. We will create a series of reference distributions from the beginning of each calendar year of equal length to the current distribution. This just uses NNS.reg(..., order = "max") which is a knn surrogate, and k=1 in this classification instance.

First, a quick test to see if using the current year actually returns the current year…

returns_list <- list()
last_year <- current_year

for(i in seq(1950,last_year,1)){
    index <- which(i == seq(1950,last_year,1))
    returns_list[[index]] <- reference_returns[eval(as.character(i))][1:w]
}

IV <- matrix(unlist(returns_list), ncol = w, byrow = TRUE)
DV <- seq(1950,last_year,1)



nns.estimate <- NNS.reg(IV, DV, point.est = t(current_returns), order = "max", n.best = 1, 
                        residual.plot = FALSE, type = "CLASS")$Point.est

nns.estimate
## [1] 2026

Yup, exact match! Let’s remove the current_year from the returns_list.

returns_list <- list()
last_year <- current_year - 1

for(i in seq(1950,last_year,1)){
    index <- which(i == seq(1950,last_year,1))
    returns_list[[index]] <- reference_returns[eval(as.character(i))][1:w]
}

IV <- matrix(unlist(returns_list), ncol = w, byrow = TRUE)
DV <- seq(1950,last_year,1)



nns.estimate <- NNS.reg(IV, DV, point.est = t(current_returns), order = "max", n.best = 1, 
                        residual.plot = FALSE, type = "CLASS")$Point.est

nns.estimate 
## [1] 1965
# View the plot on both series
plot(as.zoo(reference[as.character(nns.estimate)][1:w]), col = c("blue"), xlab = "Date", ylab = "Price",
     main = paste("NNS \n Most Similar Calendar Year \n", nns.estimate))
par(new =TRUE)
plot(as.zoo(current),screens = 1,lwd = 3, col = "red",xlab = "",ylab = "", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n")
axis(4)
mtext("Price", side = 4, line = 3)
legend("topleft",c("Reference","Current (RHS)"),lty = c(1,1),col = c("blue","red"),cex = 0.5, bty = "n")

# Future from most similar period
future_GSPC <- reference[as.character(nns.estimate)][w:min((2*w),length(reference[as.character(nns.estimate)]))]
plot(future_GSPC)

Finding the Most Similar Period (Non-Calendar Year)

Next we will eschew the calendar year and scan overlapping years to find the most similar period. The independent variable matrices get excessive (since each observation is an IV and they sequentially overlap), so we can simplify by minimizing the sum-of-squared differences, or maximizing the linear correlation of vectors to determine similarity.

Use any length of latest returns

We will use the last 77 trading days.

#current_returns <- tail(current_returns, 60) #Set to any length
w <- length(current_returns)

Remove current period, also a verification of similarity!

If we do not remove the last w observations from the reference data, we will match exactly to the current starting period.

# Measure time
start.time <- Sys.time()

best.period.1 <- which.max(
  sapply(
    seq_len(length(reference_returns) - length(current_returns) + 1),
    function(i) cor(as.numeric(reference_returns[i:(i + length(current_returns) - 1)]),
                    as.numeric(current_returns))
  )
)

# Calculate elapsed time
print(Sys.time() - start.time)
## Time difference of 1.401255 secs
# Output the best matching period's value in GSPC
GSPC[best.period.1]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 2026-01-02   6878.11   6894.87  6824.31    6858.47  4184120000       6858.47

Yup, exact match! Let’s remove those current observations from the reference.

# Trim both reference series together to keep them in sync
reference        <- head(reference,        nrow(reference)        - w)
reference_returns <- head(reference_returns, length(reference_returns) - w)

Method 1: Linear Correlation and Normalized Returns Data

The first method we will use is a regular linear correlation of the daily returns data.

best.period.1 <- which.max(
  sapply(
    seq_len(length(reference_returns) - length(current_returns) + 1),
    function(i) cor(as.numeric(reference_returns[i:(i + length(current_returns) - 1)]),
                    as.numeric(current_returns))
  )
)

# Most similar period
GSPC[c(best.period.1, best.period.1+w)]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 1991-05-28    377.49    382.10   377.12     381.94   162350000        381.94
## 1991-09-16    383.59    385.79   382.77     385.78   172560000        385.78
# View Plot on Both Series
plot(as.zoo(reference[best.period.1:(best.period.1+w)]), col = c("blue"), xlab = "Date", ylab = "Price",
     main = paste("LINEAR CORRELATION \n Most Similar Period \n", index(reference_returns[best.period.1]), " : ", index(reference_returns[(best.period.1+w)])))
par(new =TRUE)
plot(as.zoo(current),screens = 1,lwd = 3, col = "red", xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n")
axis(4)
mtext("Price", side = 4, line = 3)
legend("topleft",c("Reference","Current (RHS)"), lty = c(1,1), col = c("blue","red"), cex = 0.5, bty = "n")

# Future from most similar period
GSPC[c(best.period.1+w,best.period.1+(2*w))]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 1991-09-16    383.59    385.79   382.77     385.78   172560000        385.78
## 1992-01-06    419.31    419.44   416.92     417.96   251210000        417.96
future_GSPC_1 <- reference[(best.period.1+w):(best.period.1+(2*w))]
plot(future_GSPC_1)

# SSE
sum( (as.numeric(reference_returns[best.period.1:(best.period.1-1+w)]) - as.numeric(current_returns))^2 )
## [1] 0.005823942

Method 2: Sum-of-Squared Differences of Daily Returns

The second method again uses the daily returns, but will sum their squared differences.

Accuracy Check

First, let’s check its accuracy on the complete dataset to see if it selects the current period as the most likely period…

# Reload full series for accuracy check — reset both price and returns together
reference_returns_full <- dailyReturn(GSPC[-1], type = "arithmetic")

best.period.2 <- which.min(
  sapply(
    seq_len(length(reference_returns_full) - length(current_returns) + 1),
    function(i) sum((as.numeric(reference_returns_full[i:(i + length(current_returns) - 1)]) - as.numeric(current_returns))^2)
  )
)

# Output the most similar period's value in GSPC
GSPC[best.period.2]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 2025-12-31   6898.82   6901.42  6844.55     6845.5  3261830000        6845.5

Yup, it works!

Apply Sum-of-Squared Differences to Daily Returns

Now we will apply the sum-of-squared differences to the daily returns data, after removing the current observations from the reference…again.

# reference_returns already has current period removed (from `remove` chunk)
best.period.2 <- which.min(
  sapply(
    seq_len(length(reference_returns) - length(current_returns) + 1),
    function(i) sum((as.numeric(reference_returns[i:(i + length(current_returns) - 1)]) - as.numeric(current_returns))^2)
  )
)

# Most similar period
GSPC[c(best.period.2, best.period.2+w)]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 1952-07-30     25.37     25.37    25.37      25.37     1240000         25.37
## 1952-11-20     25.28     25.28    25.28      25.28     1740000         25.28
# View Plot on Both Series
plot(as.zoo(reference[best.period.2:(best.period.2+w)]),lty = 1, col = c("blue"), xlab = "Date", ylab = "Price",
     main = paste("SUM OF SQUARED DIFFERENCES \n Most Similar Period \n", index(reference_returns[best.period.2]), " : ", index(reference_returns[(best.period.2+w)])))
par(new =TRUE)
plot(as.zoo(current), screens = 1, lwd = 3, col = "red", xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n")
axis(4)
mtext("Price", side = 4, line = 3)
legend("topleft", c("Reference","Current"), lty = c(1,1), col = c("blue","red"), cex = 0.5, bty = "n")

# Future from most similar period
GSPC[c(best.period.2+w, best.period.2+(2*w))]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 1952-11-20     25.28     25.28    25.28      25.28     1740000         25.28
## 1953-03-16     26.22     26.22    26.22      26.22     1770000         26.22
future_GSPC_2 <- reference[(best.period.2+w):(best.period.2+(2*w))]
plot(future_GSPC_2)

# SSE
sum( (as.numeric(reference_returns[best.period.2:(best.period.2-1+w)]) - as.numeric(current_returns))^2 )
## [1] 0.005533391

Comments

  • Evaluating each of the methods most similar daily returns via the minimum sum-of-squared errors, reveals Method #2 has the best fit.
  • We have not ventured far into the definition of \(similar\). We have demonstrated 2 methods of determining similarity, and unfortunately, the future outcomes are substantially varied based on the definition and evaluation criteria.
  • Based on prevailing evaluation criteria, both future outcomes are significantly positive from current levels for the next 77 day period
# View Plot on Both Series
plot(as.zoo(future_GSPC_1), col = c("blue"), xlab = "Date", ylab = "Price", main = "Future Performance for Similar Periods")
par(new =TRUE)
plot(as.zoo(future_GSPC_2), screens = 1, lwd = 3, col = "red", xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n")
axis(4)
mtext("Price", side = 4, line = 3)
legend("topleft", c("Future via Method #1 (LHS)","Future via Method #2 (RHS)"), lty = c(1,1), col = c("blue","red"), cex = 0.5 , bty = "n")

Other Similarity Measures

I have included the binary classification of the most similar period and a dynamic time warping. The binary classification is simply the percentage of concordant tuples sum(x<0 & y<0 | x>0 & y>0) / length(x). First, we will check their accuracy.

custom_cor_2 <- function(x, y){
  a <- sum(as.numeric(x) > 0 & as.numeric(y) > 0 | as.numeric(x) < 0 & as.numeric(y) < 0) / length(x)
  return(a)
}



# Reload full series for accuracy check
reference_returns_full <- dailyReturn(GSPC[-1], type = "arithmetic")

best.period.3 <- which.max(
  sapply(
    seq_len(length(reference_returns_full) - length(current_returns) + 1),
    function(i) custom_cor_2(reference_returns_full[i:(i + length(current_returns) - 1)], current_returns)
  )
)

# Most similar period
GSPC[best.period.3]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 2025-12-31   6898.82   6901.42  6844.55     6845.5  3261830000        6845.5
require(TSdist)

best.period.4 <- which.min(
  sapply(
    seq_len(length(reference_returns_full) - length(current_returns) + 1),
    function(i) TSdist::DTWDistance(reference_returns_full[i:(i + length(current_returns) - 1)], current_returns)
  )
)

# Most similar period
GSPC[best.period.4]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 2025-12-31   6898.82   6901.42  6844.55     6845.5  3261830000        6845.5

Yup, they both pass the accuracy check. Now let’s apply to the rest of the series after removing the current observations…

# reference_returns already has current period removed (from `remove` chunk)

best.period.3 <- which.max(
  sapply(
    seq_len(length(reference_returns) - length(current_returns) + 1),
    function(i) custom_cor_2(reference_returns[i:(i + length(current_returns) - 1)], current_returns)
  )
)

# Most similar period
GSPC[c(best.period.3, best.period.3+w)]
##            GSPC.Open GSPC.High GSPC.Low GSPC.Close GSPC.Volume GSPC.Adjusted
## 1966-06-15     87.07     87.74    86.33      86.73     8520000         86.73
## 1966-10-04     74.90     75.76    73.91      75.10     8910000         75.10

par(mfrow=c(2,2))

# View Plot on Both Series

par(new =TRUE)

Again, different definitions of similarity will yield different periods of association.

Future Paths

par(mfrow=c(2,2))

future_GSPC_1 <- reference[(best.period.1+w):(best.period.1+(2*w))]
plot(future_GSPC_1)

future_GSPC_2 <- reference[(best.period.2+w):(best.period.2+(2*w))]
plot(future_GSPC_2)
